grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: Dictionary/lemma form is ਗੁਰੂ (Guru). ਗੁਰ is the frequent oblique or compounding form used before another noun (e.g., ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ, "by the Guru's grace"), while the aunkar-marked ਗੁਰੁ signals nominative case in careful Gurbani orthography.
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: The final vowel sign (aunkar ੁ) tracks case: ਗੁਰੁ (with aunkar) generally functions as subject/nominative; ਗੁਰ (without aunkar) functions as an oblique form before a postposition or as the first member of a compound (ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ, ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ).
grammar.sentence_function: Functions as subject, object, or first member of a compound depending on the case ending present; recurs in all these slots throughout SGGS.
grammar.authority: Prof. Sahib Singh, Gurbani Viakaran (grammatical framework for lagaan-matra case distinctions in SGGS)

senses.attested_meaning: A teacher; one who removes ignorance/darkness and gives spiritual instruction.
senses.usage_note: Used for a living human teacher in the ordinary sense, for the ten Sikh Gurus specifically, and increasingly through the text for the Shabad/Word itself as the real locus of teaching authority.

textual_evidence.verse_gurmukhi: ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ ॥
textual_evidence.verse_transliteration: Ik Onkar Sat Naam Karta Purakh Nirbhau Nirvair Akal Murat Ajooni Saibhang Gur Prasad
textual_evidence.author: Guru Nanak Dev Ji (Mahala 1)
textual_evidence.source: Recalled from memory. Mool Mantar's fixed position at Ang 1 is essentially universal across standard (Damdami Bir) printings, but this was not independently re-verified against a live corpus this session.

components: guru — a single root, not compositionally analyzable as gu+ru in standard Sanskrit grammar
candidates.root_meaning: "heavy, weighty" — by extension, one whose authority/knowledge carries weight
candidates.authority: Monier-Williams Sanskrit-English Dictionary; Mahan Kosh (Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha), which also separately notes the popular 'gu' (darkness) + 'ru' (light) gloss as a later devotional folk etymology, not a Sanskrit grammatical fact

linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: The Sanskrit root sense ('weighty, heavy [with authority]') is a general honorific for any teacher across Indian traditions. Gurbani usage narrows and elevates it into a specific theological category — the Guru as the necessary channel for Naam and liberation, and eventually the Shabad/scripture itself — a much narrower, more load-bearing sense than the general Sanskrit honorific.

adaptation_note.text: Kabir ji and other Bhagats inherit the same pan-Indian Sanskrit honorific for 'teacher' already current in Bhakti and Nath-yogic circles before Guru Nanak. Gurbani's distinct contribution is institutionalizing the title across ten specific successors and finally the scripture itself, not coining the word.

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: Structurally, 'Gur/Guru' names an external reference point outside the self-referential loop of Man/Haumai — a fixed point of address the practitioner can orient toward instead of the mind's own recursive self-tracking. The grammatical fact that the word shifts case (subject vs. oblique 'of/by the Guru') mirrors this: it is used both as an active agent and as a source one receives from, modeling a relationship rather than a self-generated state.

sources: memory recall of Mool Mantar text — not independently corpus-verified this session

grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: Lemma ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ. The same nominative/oblique case pattern as Gur/Guru applies to its second member, so ਸਤਿਗੁਰ appears before postpositions or a second noun (ਸਤਿਗੁਰ ਕੀ ਸੇਵਾ — "service of the Satguru").
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: Aunkar on the final syllable marks nominative case (ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ); its absence marks oblique/possessive constructions — identical mechanism to Gur/Guru.
grammar.sentence_function: Functions grammatically like Guru — subject, object, or first member of further compounds — with 'Sat' as a fixed, non-inflecting first member.

senses.attested_meaning: The True Guru/Teacher — used for God directly, for the Guru's realized inner state, and for the ten historical Gurus.
senses.usage_note: Distinguishes a genuine, truth-grounded teacher from a false or self-appointed one.

textual_evidence.verse_gurmukhi: ਅਨੰਦੁ ਭਇਆ ਮੇਰੀ ਮਾਏ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ ਮੈ ਪਾਇਆ ॥
textual_evidence.verse_transliteration: Anand bhaya meri mae Satguru mai paaiaa
textual_evidence.author: Guru Amar Das Ji (Mahala 3)
textual_evidence.source: Recalled from memory as the opening line of Anand Sahib — widely known, but exact Ang not independently verified this session.

candidates.root_meaning: a teacher who is [grounded in] truth/true being
candidates.authority: Mahan Kosh; standard Sanskrit compounding rules

linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: Grammatically transparent as 'true Guru' in both Sanskrit and Gurbani — one of the few terms in this batch with almost no gap between root and usage, though Gurbani sharpens 'true' to mean specifically God-realized/God-identical rather than merely honest.

adaptation_note.text: Kabir ji's dohas use 'Satguru' for an inwardly realized teacher, sometimes explicitly distinguished from any physical/human teacher — a Sant-tradition usage that runs parallel to Guru Bani's own usage rather than being borrowed from it.

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: The 'Sat' prefix functions as a verification-flag on the Gur-relationship: it marks the external reference point as non-illusory, guarding against the mind's own opinions being relabeled as guidance (a Haumai/Maya substitution).
operational_reading.grounded_in: the attested 'true teacher, God-realized' sense above

sources: memory recall of Anand Sahib opening — not independently corpus-verified this session

grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: Lemma ਸਬਦੁ. The sihari-marked instrumental form ਸਬਦਿ ("through/by the Shabad") is extremely frequent and grammatically distinct from the plain oblique ਸਬਦ.
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: The instrumental/locative sihari ending is one of the most theologically significant markers for this word — 'ਸਬਦਿ ਮਰੈ' ("dies through/by the Shabad") is grammatically distinct from a plain nominative or oblique occurrence, shifting the sense from 'the Shabad [as topic]' to 'by means of the Shabad.'
grammar.sentence_function: Frequently the instrumental means by which an action (dying to ego, merging, awakening) is accomplished, not merely the grammatical subject or object.
grammar.authority: Prof. Sahib Singh, Gurbani Viakaran (treatment of the sihari-marked instrumental case)

senses.usage_note: Used straightforwardly for an individual composition when discussing the text's own structure.

textual_evidence.source: No single-line citation needed for this structural/self-referential sense; attested by the text's own organizing convention (shabads as titled units within each raag section) rather than one verse.

senses.attested_meaning: The Word/sound-principle through which truth is revealed and by which the ego is directly acted upon.
senses.usage_note: Carried specifically by the instrumental sihari form (ਸਬਦਿ) rather than the plain noun; this is where the term does the most theological/operative work in the text.

textual_evidence.verse_gurmukhi: ਗੁਰ ਕਾ ਸਬਦੁ ਵਸੈ ਮਨਿ ਆਇ ॥
textual_evidence.verse_transliteration: Gur ka sabad vasai man aae
textual_evidence.author: Guru Amar Das Ji (Mahala 3)
textual_evidence.source: Recalled as a representative recurring phrase-pattern in SGGS ("gur ka sabad ... man"), not one verified single occurrence — flagged for corpus confirmation of exact wording and location.

components: शब्द — a single root, not further decomposed in standard Sanskrit grammar

linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: The Sanskrit root is a general linguistic/acoustic term (any sound or word). Gurbani usage narrows it to a specific soteriological category — the Guru's revealed utterance treated as causally efficacious (something one 'dies through' or is 'immersed in') — a much stronger operative claim than the neutral root meaning.

adaptation_note.text: The philosophical weight of śabda as a near-ontological category (śabda-brahman — reality construed as sound/word) is already present in classical Vedanta and grammar-philosophy prior to Guru Nanak. Kabir ji's shabads carry the same operative sense of the Word as an active force, suggesting the concept is inherited from wider Sant-Bhakti/Vedantic discourse rather than coined within Gurbani.

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: The instrumental case marking (Sabadi) structurally positions the Shabad as the operator/tool that acts on the self ('dies through the Shabad'), not an object the self acts upon. This supports reading Sabad as an intervention applied to the Man/Haumai system from outside its own loop, rather than a belief the mind adopts within the same loop.

grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: Functions largely as an invariant compound noun — it does not show the same nominative/oblique aunkar alternation as Gur/Sabad. Appears mostly in constructions like ਹਉਮੈ ਵਿਚਿ ("within haumai") or ਹਉਮੈ ਮਾਰਿ ("striking down haumai").
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: Unlike Gur/Sabad, Haumai's own ending does not carry a nominative/oblique contrast; grammatical variability shows up instead in the surrounding verbs and postpositions (marai, gavaiye, vichi).
grammar.sentence_function: Typically the object of a verb of destruction/loss (marna "to die to", gavauna "to lose") or the locative field within which something happens — rarely the grammatical subject performing an action itself.

senses.attested_meaning: Egotism — the self-referential 'I-am-I' sense named as the central obstacle to God-realization.
senses.usage_note: Named directly as a 'disease' (rog) in a well-known couplet, with its own remedy said to lie within it via the Shabad.

textual_evidence.verse_gurmukhi: ਹਉਮੈ ਦੀਰਘ ਰੋਗੁ ਹੈ ਦਾਰੂ ਭੀ ਇਸੁ ਮਾਹਿ ॥
textual_evidence.verse_transliteration: Haumai deeragh rog hai daaru bhee is maahi
textual_evidence.author: Guru Amar Das Ji (Mahala 3)
textual_evidence.source: Recalled from memory as a widely cited couplet in Sikh teaching; exact Ang/raag placement not independently verified this session.

candidates.original_script_form: अहं (ahaṁ, "I") doubled with a first-person oblique form
components: ਹਉ (hau, "I" — from Sanskrit अहम् ahám via Prakrit अहं ahaṁ)
candidates.authority: Mahan Kosh notes the doubled first-person derivation; this is the standard scholarly account, though a second independent linguistic source was not cross-checked this session

linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: The root is a grammatical curiosity — two first-person pronoun forms fused, rather than a philosophical term borrowed wholesale (unlike Sabad or Karam). Gurbani usage turns this grammatical doubling into the proper name of a specific spiritual-psychological affliction. Notably, Gurbani does NOT use the existing Sanskrit philosophical term ahamkara (अहंकार) for this concept, choosing the native doubled-pronoun compound instead — a real coinage, not a borrowed category.

adaptation_note.text: This term appears to be a Gurbani-internal coinage rather than one adopted from an identifiable external source text. I do not have confident evidence of Kabir ji or other Bhagats using this exact compound as heavily as the Guru Sahiban do, and flag this for corpus verification rather than asserting cross-Bhagat usage I'm not sure of.

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: Grammatically, Haumai is almost never the subject of a sentence — it is what is acted upon (killed, lost, dissolved) or the field within which something happens. This matches a reading of Haumai as a recursive tracking-process (a doubled self-reference, 'I' referring to 'me') rather than an entity or agent — consistent with treating it as a loop to interrupt rather than an opponent to defeat.
operational_reading.grounded_in: the attested 'doubled first-person, self-referential obstacle' sense above

sources: memory recall — several details flagged medium/low confidence and not independently corpus-verified this session

grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: Lemma ਹੁਕਮੁ. The sihari-marked instrumental/locative form ਹੁਕਮਿ ("by/through/within the Order") is the most theologically loaded form, distinct from the plain nominative.
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: As with Sabad, the sihari-marked instrumental form shifts the word from naming the Order as a topic to describing something as happening 'within' or 'by means of' it — e.g. ਹੁਕਮੈ ਅੰਦਰਿ ਸਭੁ ਕੋ ("all are within the Hukam") uses a further-inflected locative.
grammar.sentence_function: Frequently the locative field ('within the Hukam') rather than a direct grammatical object — a similar 'field word' pattern to Haumai, though for the opposite theological reason (Hukam encompasses; Haumai afflicts).

senses.attested_meaning: Command, in the everyday administrative/legal sense.
senses.usage_note: Retains a plain administrative sense in some occurrences, distinct from the cosmic-order sense.

textual_evidence.source: No specific citation identified this session for the plain administrative sense in isolation from the cosmic-order sense; flagged for corpus search.

senses.attested_meaning: The Divine Order/Will — the encompassing law within which all created things exist and move.
senses.usage_note: The dominant sense in Japji Sahib's opening pauris, where grasping Hukam is presented as the direct answer to the composition's opening question about becoming sachiar.

textual_evidence.verse_gurmukhi: ਹੁਕਮੈ ਅੰਦਰਿ ਸਭੁ ਕੋ ਬਾਹਰਿ ਹੁਕਮਿ ਨ ਕੋਇ ॥
textual_evidence.verse_transliteration: Hukamai andar sabh ko baahar hukam na koe
textual_evidence.author: Guru Nanak Dev Ji (Mahala 1)
textual_evidence.source: Recalled from memory as Japji Sahib, Pauri 1. Its placement on Ang 1 follows from the Mool Mantar and opening pauris' fixed position in standard SGGS pagination, but was not independently re-verified against a live corpus this session.

components: ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m) triliteral root, "to judge, to rule, to be wise"
candidates.root_meaning: a judgment, ruling, or command issued by an authority
candidates.authority: standard Arabic lexicography (ḥ-k-m root); Mahan Kosh confirms the Persian/Arabic administrative-loanword derivation into Punjabi

linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: The root is narrowly administrative/legal — a ruler's specific decree. Gurbani usage stretches this into a cosmological category covering the entirety of natural and moral law — a gap of scale (a particular command → universal Order), not of kind.

adaptation_note.text: I do not have confident recall of Kabir ji, Ravidas ji, or Farid ji using this specific Persian-administrative term as a load-bearing theological category the way Guru Nanak does in Japji Sahib; Farid ji's bani draws on a different, more directly Quranic/Sufi vocabulary (e.g. Rabb) for divine authority. Flagged as Guru-Nanak-specific pending a corpus check across the Bhagat Bani.

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: Grammatically encompassing (things exist 'within' Hukam, locative case) rather than imposed on an external object, Hukam structurally reframes the self as already inside a governing order rather than a separate agent negotiating with one. The text pairs recognizing this directly with the loss of Haumai in the same couplet, suggesting the 'operation' here is a reframing of location (inside vs. outside a system) rather than an addition of belief.
operational_reading.grounded_in: the attested 'encompassing Divine Order' sense above, and its direct textual pairing with Haumai in Japji Sahib Pauri 1

sources: memory recall of Japji Sahib Pauri 1 — not independently corpus-verified this session

grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: Lemma ਸੁਰਤਿ. Behaves as a feminine noun with comparatively stable ending across cases, appearing frequently in construct with a verb of joining/attaching (ਸੁਰਤਿ ਸਮਾਲਿ — "attend to/gather the surat") or instrumentally paired with Sabad (ਸੁਰਤਿ ਸਬਦਿ — "consciousness [attuned] through the Shabad").
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: The sihari-final form is comparatively stable across occurrences — feminine nouns in Gurbani generally show less case-marking variation than masculine ones like Gur/Sabad/Hukam. The grammatical action is carried more by the accompanying postposition/verb than by inflection of Surat itself.
grammar.sentence_function: Usually the subject or topic of an action of attending, merging, or attuning — frequently paired instrumentally with Sabad to describe the mechanism of attunement.

senses.attested_meaning: Consciousness, attention, or the faculty of awareness that can be focused/attuned.
senses.usage_note: Frequently combined with Shabad as 'Surat Shabad' naming the specific practice/state of attuning consciousness to the Word.

textual_evidence.author: Guru Nanak Dev Ji (Mahala 1)
textual_evidence.source: Recalled from memory as a well-known line from Siddh Gosht (Guru Nanak's recorded dialogue with the Nath yogis); exact Ang not independently verified this session.

candidates.original_script_form: सुरति (surati), possibly सु (su-, "well") + रति (rati, "resting in, delight")
candidates.authority: one line of Punjabi lexicographic treatment; not independently cross-checked against Mahan Kosh this session

candidates.root_meaning: "hearing, that which is heard/revealed", on this alternate candidate derivation
candidates.authority: an alternate derivation connecting Surat to the general Indic root for hearing/revelation; not independently cross-checked this session

linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: Whichever specific Sanskrit root is correct, Gurbani usage narrows 'surat' to a specific technical sense: the directed, trainable faculty of awareness that can be attuned to the Shabad — closer to a technical term for 'the listening/attending function of consciousness' than to either candidate root's general meaning alone. The origin itself is flagged disputed rather than asserted as settled.

adaptation_note.text: 'Surat' appears prominently in Siddh Gosht, a composition explicitly staged as Guru Nanak's dialogue with Nath yogis. The term (attention/consciousness as a trainable faculty) is common currency in Nath-yogic vocabulary — surat-shabad-yoga is a recognized later Sant/Nath technical term — so Guru Nanak may be engaging existing Nath terminology rather than introducing a new concept.

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: If Surat names a trainable, directable faculty of attention distinct from Man (the mind) and Haumai (self-referential tracking), the operative claim is that awareness itself can be redirected away from self-tracking and toward the Shabad as an object of attunement — treating attention as a lever separate from belief-content or willpower.
operational_reading.grounded_in: the attested 'directed faculty of awareness attuned to Shabad' sense above

sources: memory recall of Siddh Gosht — not independently corpus-verified this session

grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: Lemma ਨਾਦੁ. Instrumental/locative ਨਾਦਿ marks 'through/by sound' constructions, paralleling Sabad's grammatical behavior.
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: Same aunkar/sihari case system as Gur/Sabad/Hukam: ਨਾਦੁ nominative vs ਨਾਦਿ instrumental.
grammar.sentence_function: Often paired with Naam and Ved in cumulative/list constructions (e.g. the Vismaad pauri) rather than standing as a sole grammatical subject.

senses.attested_meaning: Sound, sound-current — used both for musical/cosmic sound and, compounded as 'Anhad Naad', the 'unstruck' inner sound.
senses.usage_note: Appears independently (as an object of wonder, e.g. the Vismaad pauri) and compounded with 'Anhad' as a specific meditative-technical term.

textual_evidence.author: Guru Nanak Dev Ji (Mahala 1)
textual_evidence.source: Recalled from memory, Japji Sahib Pauri 16, on Ang 1 per standard SGGS pagination (Japji Sahib spans Ang 1-8); not independently re-verified against a live corpus this session.

components: नाद — single root, from नद् (nad, "to sound, roar")

linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: The Sanskrit root is a general acoustic term. Its specific technical use in the compound 'Anhad Naad' (unstruck sound) draws on a much narrower classical yogic/Nath cosmological doctrine (nāda as a stage of subtle sound in nada-yoga systems) rather than the general Sanskrit word alone.

adaptation_note.text: Kabir ji, closely engaged with Nath-yogic circles, uses 'Naad' (and 'Anhad Naad') in the same technical sense inherited from Nath meditative doctrine — adopted terminology from that tradition rather than a Gurbani-internal coinage.

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: As a component of 'Anhad Naad' (sound with no external striking cause), Naad structurally names an internally-arising signal not produced by ordinary cause-and-effect contact — a marker or target distinct from the mind's own generated noise (thought, haumai-chatter), something to attune Surat toward rather than something the mind manufactures.
operational_reading.grounded_in: the attested Anhad Naad technical sense above

sources: memory recall of Japji Sahib Pauri 16 — not independently corpus-verified this session

grammar.part_of_speech: adjective (used substantivally as "one who is guru-less")
grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: Formed by prefixing the negative/privative ਨਿ (ni-) to ਗੁਰ (gur, oblique form of guru) plus the adjectival kanna (ਾ) ending characteristic of Punjabi -a stem adjectives (cf. ਕਾਲਾ kala, "black").
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: The kanna-ending marks it grammatically as an adjective inflecting for gender/number like other -a stem adjectives (ਨਿਗੁਰਾ masc. sg., ਨਿਗੁਰੇ oblique/plural) — a distinct system from the nominative/oblique noun-case pattern of Guru itself.
grammar.sentence_function: Functions predicatively or attributively, describing a person as lacking a Guru/being unguided — generally in a cautionary or negative register.
grammar.authority: Prof. Sahib Singh, Gurbani Viakaran (treatment of ni- privative adjective formations)

senses.attested_meaning: One without a Guru; guideless, spiritually unguided.
senses.usage_note: Used to describe the condition of a person cut off from Guru-guidance, generally negatively.

textual_evidence.source: I recall this term occurring in Gurbani in warning contexts but could not confidently reconstruct a specific verse this session without risk of misquoting. Flagged for corpus lookup rather than invented.

candidates.authority: Mahan Kosh; standard Punjabi privative adjective formation (ni- + noun + -a)

linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: Essentially no gap — this is a transparent, compositionally clear formation whose Gurbani sense matches its grammatical construction directly.

authors_who_use_it: Gurbani generally — specific author/composition attribution not independently verified this session

adaptation_note.text: I do not have a specific, confidently-recalled Bhagat occurrence of this exact term to report. Flagged for verification rather than asserting Bhagat usage I'm unsure of.

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: Naming the state of being 'unguided' as a specific, nameable condition (rather than simply 'wrong' or 'sinful') structurally implies the default/untrained state of Man is disconnected from any external reference point — consistent with reading Haumai not as a moral failure so much as the default condition of a system running without Gur/Sabad input.
operational_reading.grounded_in: the attested 'without a Guru' sense above

sources: Prof. Sahib Singh, Gurbani Viakaran (privative adjective formation)
no specific verse citation available this session

grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: Base form ਸਹਜ functions as noun ('a state of Sahaj') or adjective. The adverbial form ਸਹਜੇ (with added vowel) is extremely common, modifying a verb of action (e.g. patterns like 'sahaje aavai sahaje jaavai', roughly "comes/goes spontaneously").
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: The added final vowel in ਸਹਜੇ marks the adverbial function, grammatically distinct from the bare noun/adjective ਸਹਜ — this shift from noun to adverb is a significant grammatical fact often collapsed when the word is translated as a single English noun ('equipoise').
grammar.sentence_function: As adverb, modifies the manner of an action (spontaneously, without effort); as noun, names the resulting state itself.

senses.attested_meaning: A state of innate, effortless balance/poise; also functions adverbially meaning 'spontaneously, naturally, without strain.'
senses.usage_note: The adverbial form (Sahaje) is at least as frequent as the nominal form in SGGS and should not be collapsed into a single 'noun' gloss.

textual_evidence.source: I recall the adverbial pattern ('sahaje ... sahaje') recurring across multiple shabads but could not confidently reconstruct one specific verse without risk of conflating separate occurrences. Flagged for corpus lookup rather than invented.

components: ज (ja, "born" — from जन् jan, "to be born")
candidates.root_meaning: "born together with" — hence "innate, natural, arising spontaneously with [something]"

linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: The compositional root meaning ('born-together-with', i.e. innate) matches Gurbani usage closely for the noun/adjective sense. The specific grammatical extension into an adverb of manner (Sahaje, "effortlessly") is a Punjabi-internal grammatical development, not already present as such in the Sanskrit source.

adaptation_note.text: 'Sahaja' was already a key technical term of the Nath yogis and the wider Sahajiya Tantric-Bhakti currents (naming a distinct meditative attainment) before Guru Nanak or Kabir ji use it; both appear to be engaging existing Nath/Sahajiya vocabulary rather than introducing a new term.

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: The grammatical fact that Sahaj most often appears as an adverb of manner (how an action happens) rather than a state one arrives at and stops, suggests it names a mode of ongoing functioning ('happening sahaje') rather than a final achieved endpoint — compatible with reading the goal as a change in how the Man/Surat system operates moment to moment, not a one-time permanent switch.

sources: no specific verse citation independently verified this session

grammar.part_of_speech: verb (not a noun) — root ਚੀਨਣਾ/ਚੀਨ੍ਹਣਾ (cheenna/cheenhna, "to recognize, examine, discern")
grammar.lemma_vs_inflected: The infinitive/lemma is ਚੀਨਣਾ (cheenna). ਚੀਨਸਿ is a specific finite inflected form; per Sahib Singh's grammar, -ਸਿ endings on verbs generally mark a general/habitual or optative present sense, roughly "[one] recognizes / may [one] recognize" — distinct from the imperative ਚੀਨਹੁ or the absolutive ਚੀਨ੍ਹਿ.
grammar.lagaan_matra_note: The ਸਿ ending here is a verb-conjugation marker, not a noun case-ending — grammatically unlike every noun entry in this batch (Gur, Satgur, Sabad, Haumai, Hukam, Surat, Naad) and should not be analyzed with the nominative/oblique noun framework.
grammar.sentence_function: Functions as the main verb of a clause, typically instructing or describing the act of recognizing/discerning something (often the Self, Hukam, or the Shabad) rather than naming a concept as a noun would.
grammar.authority: Prof. Sahib Singh, Gurbani Viakaran (treatment of verb-ending conjugation patterns including -si forms)

senses.attested_meaning: To recognize, discern, or examine closely — most often used with reference to recognizing one's own true nature/origin or Hukam.
senses.usage_note: Frequently used in address to the reader/listener as an instruction to actively examine or recognize something, not to describe a passive state.

textual_evidence.source: I recall this root verb occurring in instructive contexts (e.g. being told to recognize one's own Self/origin) but could not confidently reconstruct the exact verse carrying this specific -si inflected form without risk of error. linguistic_origin.root_vs_usage_gap: Regardless of which Sanskrit root is correct, Gurbani usage clearly means an active, discerning 'recognition/examination' (of the Self, of Hukam, of one's own origin) rather than passive perception — closer to 'actively identify/discern' than to simple 'see' or 'know.'

operational_reading.layer: INTERPRETIVE — a structural reading, not the attested meaning
operational_reading.reading: As an imperative/instructive verb rather than a noun naming a state, 'Cheenas'-type forms structurally frame realization as an act the practitioner is directed to perform (examine, discern, identify) repeatedly, rather than a status conferred or a thing possessed — shifting the operative frame from 'having' a realization to 'doing' an ongoing act of recognition.
